analysis.one_liner: Hands endangered species protection to states and requires Congress to approve every federal species listing.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a hearing or a vote: introduced with one cosponsor in July 2019, it sat in the Senate Environment and Public Works Committee until the Congress ended in January 2021.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would rewrite the Endangered Species Act so no species could be added to the federal endangered or threatened list without the consent of every governor in its range and a vote of Congress, and all listings would expire after five years. States could take over protection of species found only within their borders, with their decisions shielded from any court review. Landowners could get clearance to develop habitat — automatically deemed compliant if the Interior Department missed a 90-day deadline — and collect 150% of property value when a federal action cut a property's value in half. It would also strip attorney fees from citizen enforcement suits and allow ranchers to kill black vultures threatening livestock.
analysis.who_benefits: Owners and developers of land that harbors endangered species, ranchers losing livestock to black vultures, and states wanting control over wildlife within their borders. Listing would require a governor's consent and a vote of Congress, every listing would sunset after five years, an unresponsive agency would lose the power to block a proposed land use, and property owners could collect 150% of fair market value when federal protection rules cut a property's worth in half.

how_it_helps.text: No species could be listed as endangered or threatened without the consent of the governor of every state where it lives, and the full list would need a vote of Congress to take effect — a structural veto for any state or congressional faction that wanted a species unprotected.

Every listed species would automatically come off the list five years later unless Congress reapproved it, and states could claim exclusive authority over species found only within their borders — including on federal public lands — with no court able to review their decisions.

Landowners could ask the Interior Department whether a proposed use of their property would violate the law; if the department missed a 90-day deadline, the use would automatically be deemed legal, and an affirmative defense would shield owners who relied on a clearance.
When a federal agency action diminished the value of a property's intended use by at least 50%, the owner or lessee could collect 150% of the property's fair market value from the government.
Citizens who sued to enforce endangered species protections would no longer be able to recover attorney fees, raising the personal cost of enforcement suits.

Ranchers could kill black vultures they reasonably believed were threatening livestock, vehicles, or buildings, and states could control ravens where predation threatens recovery of imperiled species.

Federal power administrations would have to itemize each customer's share of endangered-species compliance costs — including foregone power generation — on monthly electric bills, building a visible cost record for the law.

analysis.who_pays: Species would pay first: state vetoes, a congressional approval requirement, five-year expirations, and unreviewable state control would leave federal protection largely theoretical for many species. Taxpayers would fund the 150% compensation payouts, and citizen groups would bear their own legal costs for enforcement suits. The public would lose the federal backstop for wildlife that crosses or lives in a single unwilling state.
analysis.who_pays_short: Endangered species, taxpayers, and citizen litigants

drawbacks.text: The bill's own structure would make protection optional: a single governor could block a listing in his or her state, Congress could refuse to approve the species list at all, and every approved listing would vanish after five years unless reenacted — a species could go extinct waiting for reauthorization.
State decisions over species found within one state could not be reviewed by any federal or state court, so a state could manage an imperiled species to extinction with no legal check.

The 150% compensation mandate would obligate taxpayers to pay well above market value whenever a federal protection cut a property's intended-use value in half, and the deemed-approval rule after 90 days would let protection lapse through agency inaction.
Eliminating attorney-fee recovery would price most citizens out of enforcement suits, since endangered-species cases are expensive and ordinary people rarely litigate without fee shifting.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill responds to real grievances — landowners can face heavy restrictions because of habitat, and vultures genuinely kill livestock — but its core design would hollow out the Endangered Species Act rather than reform it: a governor veto over listings, a congressional approval requirement, five-year automatic expirations, unreviewable state control, 150% compensation, and no fee recovery for citizen enforcers would together make federal protection largely theoretical. The costs fell on the side of species and the public lands and waters they share with people; the benefits were concentrated on a narrow set of property owners and ranchers. It never became law, so none of these effects took effect.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the Senate Environment and Public Works Committee the day it was introduced, and the committee never took it up before the two-year Congress ended.

narrative.text: Sen. Rand Paul introduced the bill on July 30, 2019, with Sen. Ted Cruz as its only cosponsor; it received a total of one cosponsor.
The same day, the Senate read it twice and referred it to the Committee on Environment and Public Works — the standard first step for a Senate bill.
That referral was the last action ever recorded: no hearing, no committee vote, no floor debate, and no roll call ever occurred before the 116th Congress ended on January 3, 2021.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Endangered species kept the existing federal protections the bill would have dismantled, and the landowners, developers, and ranchers the bill was written for gained nothing. The outcome left the conservation side of the ledger better off.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Wildlife; existing federal protections stayed intact

against.what_they_did: Never scheduled a hearing, markup, or vote on the bill during the two years it had jurisdiction; the referral was the bill's final action.

against.name: John Barrasso

sides.party_line_note: No vote ever occurred; support never extended beyond the two Republican senators, Paul and Cruz, so no partisan breakdown was ever recorded.

industries.note: The bill would have let them develop habitat with a 90-day deemed-compliance shortcut, governor vetoes over listings, five-year listing sunsets, and 150% compensation when federal rules cut property value in half. Their gain would come directly from removing the federal safeguard that keeps species habitat off the market.

The bill would have allowed killing black vultures reasonably believed to be endangering livestock — a response to real predation losses ranchers report — though it loosens protections under the Migratory Bird Treaty Act to get there.

industries.industry: Electric power industry and federal hydropower customers
industries.note: Federal power administrations would have had to show each customer's share of endangered-species compliance costs, including foregone power generation, on monthly bills. Ratepayers would see the cost drivers, but underlying obligations would not change.

Eliminating attorney-fee recovery in endangered-species suits would have raised the cost of the citizen lawsuits these groups use to force enforcement — their loss would have been the public's loss of an enforcement backstop.
